question.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}t,\,y=\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2},\,t\in [0,\sqrt{3}].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt{3}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2}t)=\frac{1}{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2})=\frac{1}{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2}t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}(1+{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{t}^{2}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=2t\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[(4)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(8-1) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
